or_adam_s_boulders.blurb: A small roadside bouldering spot on the west edge of Hills Creek Reservoir, roughly twenty minutes outside Oakridge. Around fifteen problems sit on boulders beside the road, running from easy warm-ups up to V10, with a good share of the lines in the harder range. The surface is on the slick side, which tends to favor difficult, technical lines. It catches plenty of sun, so it clears out quickly after winter wet spells and is often one of the first Willamette Valley spots to be climbable. The patch is tiny and can be partly submerged when the reservoir is high, so it suits a short session rather than a full day.

or_hunchback_2.blurb: A compact cluster of boulders tucked below the Hunchback Wall in the Mt. Hood National Forest, reached by a steep uphill trail. Around fifteen problems range from easy slab-style lines through the middle grades up to V9, so there is something for most levels even though the whole zone is small. The west-facing overhang on the main boulder is the highlight, with steep crimping. The wall above blocks the morning sun, which makes the boulders a handy summer choice when lower-elevation Gorge spots are too hot. Expect a short but strenuous walk in.
or_hunchback_2.parking_note: Pull onto the narrow shoulder on the right-hand side of Salmon River Road, just past a rock bluff; space is tight, so only a few cars fit.
or_hunchback_2.approach: From the shoulder, pick up the trail near the drainage and climb steeply; where it forks, take the more worn, steeper-looking branch. Boulders appear along the way, with the main cluster continuing right where the wall trail switches back left.

or_14_1st_alcove.blurb: A bolted alcove within the Terra Nova sport climbing zone of Southwest Oregon's Rogue Valley. Fourteen sport routes line its walls, ranging from an easy 5.7 up to the low 5.12 range, with the bulk of them in the 5.10 and 5.11 grades and a couple of 5.9s for the lower end. Several of the better-known lines here, such as La Mer, are popular across the broader area. The approach drops downhill from the crag entrance past neighboring formations before climbing back up into the alcove. Routes generally need a bit of cleaning at the start of the season.

or_turtle_rock.blurb: One of the busier blocks in the Callahans, a sandstone cliff band west of Roseburg in Southwest Oregon. Fourteen routes here are nearly all bolted, plus a single crack line, and they sit close together with plenty of link-ups. Grades run from 5.8 into 5.13, but most of the climbing is in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a few friendlier 5.9s. The rock is solid with only occasional moss. The base sits under heavy tree cover and stays shaded much of the day, while the right-hand side picks up afternoon sun. The walk in is long but not steep.

or_mean_street.blurb: A short stretch of the Rocky Butte cliffs in northeast Portland, set apart from the neighboring walls and sitting right beside the freeway, though a seasonal waterfall helps mask the traffic noise. Of its fourteen routes, most are top-rope, with a few bolted and a couple of trad lines. Grades span 5.6 to 5.13, with a decent middle chunk at 5.9 through 5.11. Rocky Butte as a whole is not a beginner crag: many routes involve rappelling in and building anchors, so it suits climbers comfortable with those skills. It is an easy after-work option within the city.

or_spiderman_buttress.blurb: A west-facing buttress on the back side of Smith Rock, known for classic moderate routes and some of the most popular climbing on that side of the park, so expect a wait on the best lines. Fourteen routes, mostly trad with a few sport lines, run from 5.4 to the 5.11 range, though the main emphasis is on the 5.7 to 5.10 grades. Its namesake multi-pitch line is a famous Smith moderate that demands smearing, jamming and nubbin pulling. Belays and ledges give wide views across the Cascade peaks.

or_main_lower_cliff.blurb: The most developed wall at Hunchback, in the Mt. Hood National Forest near Zigzag. Its fourteen routes split between trad lines (nine) and bolted faces (five), covering 5.6 through the 5.11 range, with the largest group at 5.10. Crack climbing makes up much of the trad, and a few short sport faces add variety. The crag is a quieter alternative to busier Portland-area destinations, and tall firs on the hillside bring summer shade, though they can hold moisture in early spring and late fall. The approach is a steep uphill hike.
